cards.text: This letter is written to people the writer calls “holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling.” His first ask is simple. “set your focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest whom we confess.”
Focus. Not on the group chat. Not on the bills. Not on the snooze button you hit four times this morning. On JESUS. And the writer says Jesus was faithful to the One who appointed Him.

cards.question: The writer compares Jesus to a famous name from Israel's history. Jesus was faithful to the One who appointed Him, just as ___ was faithful in all God's house.

cards.text: Moses, Israel's leader. BIG name. If Israel had a hall of fame, Moses gets his own wing. But the writer says Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses.

cards.question: To show that Jesus has greater glory than Moses, the writer uses a picture. What is it?

answers.text: A builder honored above the house
A shepherd honored above the sheep
A teacher honored above the student

cards.text: Makes sense, friend. Nobody bites a cookie and says, “Forget the baker. Give THIS cookie a trophy.” Then the writer goes bigger than one house.

cards.question: True or false: The writer says every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything.

cards.text: Now back to Moses. Moses was faithful in all God's house. Nobody's taking that from him. But the writer gives him a certain role there.

cards.question: What was Moses' role in God's house? Moses was faithful as a ___ in all God's house.

cards.text: A faithful servant, testifying to what would be spoken later. That's an important job! But Christ stands somewhere else.

cards.question: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house. How is Christ faithful?

answers.text: As the Son over God's house
As a guest inside God's house

cards.question: The writer keeps talking about God's house. Then he tells the holy brothers what God's house is. What does he say?
True or false: The writer says believers are God's house no matter what they do.

cards.text: There's an if: “we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast.” Friend, I spent YEARS stuck inside a house, back of the junk drawer, under the takeout menus. And here the writer says believers ARE the house. Talk about a promotion.
Now the writer quotes words the Holy Spirit says, from Psalm 95 (Psalm 95:7-11). They start with a word you're going to hear again: “Today.”

cards.question: The Holy Spirit's words begin, “Today, if you hear His voice,” and then comes a warning. What does it warn against?

cards.text: The words point back to the rebellion, the day of testing in the wilderness. That's where the fathers tested and tried God, even while they saw His works.

cards.question: In the wilderness, the fathers tested God while they saw His works. For how long did they see His works?

cards.text: FORTY YEARS of seeing His works. That's like watching the oven turn out perfect cookies every single day for forty years and still asking, “But are we SURE this thing gets hot?” So God was angry with that generation.

cards.question: True or false: God said that generation's hearts were finally starting to follow His ways.
God said their hearts were always going astray and they had not known His ways. So in His anger He swore an oath. What did He swear they would never enter?

cards.text: Now the writer turns from the wilderness to his own readers. And he gets personal: “See to it, brothers,”

cards.question: What kind of heart does the writer warn the brothers about?
A heart of unbelief turns away from the living God. So none of them gets hardened, what does the writer tell the brothers to do?

cards.text: DAILY. As long as it is called today. That's a group chat that actually checks on you, friend. Not the one that's been dead quiet since somebody's birthday back in March.

cards.question: True or false: The writer warns that sin is deceitful and can harden a heart.

cards.text: Sin's deceitfulness works like the snooze button. “Just five more minutes.” Then it's noon and you have NO idea where the day went. Then the writer says we have come to share in Christ, and there's an if attached.

cards.question: We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the assurance we had at first. For how long does the writer say to hold firmly?

cards.text: He quotes the Psalm again: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion.” Then he starts asking questions, like a baker checking every oven.

cards.question: The writer asks who heard and rebelled. His answer: all those ___ led out of Egypt.
The writer asks who God was angry with for forty years. His answer: those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the ___.
True or false: The writer says God swore that those who disobeyed would never enter His rest.
The writer sums it all up. It was because of their ___ that they were unable to enter.

cards.text: Unbelief. That's what kept them out. And that's why the writer keeps saying “Today.” I spent years in that junk drawer telling myself someday. So did the expired coupon I shared that drawer with. Friend, look how that turned out for the coupon.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 1 quotes "holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Hebrews 3:1 opens with "Therefore," so the passage starts in the middle of the writer's argument. The opening card never says what the "Therefore" builds on.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: "the snooze button you hit four times this morning" states something about this baker's morning and habits that Papa Dorin hasn't been told.

rule.text: What he doesn't know: anything about the individual baker that he hasn't been told, such as their streak, their mood, the time of day or how they've done before.

findings.problem: Several story cards after the opening run past 2 sentences: card 2 (6 sentences), card 4 (4), card 6 (3), card 8 (4), card 10 (3) and card 14 (4).

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card tells no part of the passage. It is only a joke reacting to 3:3 plus a teaser ("goes bigger than one house"), yet it cites Hebrews 3:3.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: "But Christ stands somewhere else" rules out the wrong answer "As a servant beside Moses" on card 11.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: No earlier card hints that being God's house is conditional, so the baker can only guess. The "if" is told afterward on card 14, which then mostly repeats answers the baker has already been given.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: "no matter what they do" frames the condition as conduct. Hebrews 3:6 makes the condition holding firmly to "our confidence and the hope of which we boast." The statement should use the text's own terms.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "even while they saw His works" adds a link of time and contrast. Hebrews 3:9 only says they "tested and tried Me, and for forty years saw My works."

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Several story cards run past 2 sentences: card 5 (3 sentences), card 11 (4), card 13 (4) and card 20 (6).

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: "that's why the writer keeps saying 'Today'" gives the writer a reason the text never states.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The joke adds to the backstory and conflicts with it. In the backstory, Papa Dorin gave up in the drawer and figured it was the end, rather than telling himself "someday." He doesn't know what happened to the coupon, but "look how that turned out for the coupon" implies he does. The punchline is also unclear about what it means.

rule.text: He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.
